questions.q: A project manager is working on a virtual project team with members from different locations. Some stakeholders are having difficulty attending meetings due to time zone differences. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Allow the stakeholders to participate in asynchronous discussions.
Inform the project sponsor of the situation and ask for guidance.
Review the organizational culture and structure to determine the best communication approach.
Reschedule meetings for different times and days.

questions.e: Understanding the organizational culture and structure will help the project manager develop a communication plan that best suits the team and stakeholders.

questions.q: A project manager is struggling to balance scope, time, and cost while maintaining project quality. If the budget is reduced, what is the most likely outcome? *

o.t: The project will still be completed on time and within scope without adjustments.
The project team must reduce scope or extend the timeline to maintain balance.
The project constraints do not affect each other.
The project quality will always remain the same, regardless of constraint changes.

questions.e: In project management, constraints are interdependent. If one constraint (e.g., budget) changes, the project manager must adjust other constraints to maintain balance. For example: If the budget is reduced, the project team may need to decrease scope or extend the schedule. If the schedule is shortened, additional resources (costs) may be needed. If scope increases, more time and budget will likely be required. This balance is essential for successful project execution.

questions.q: A company has implemented a Project Management Office (PMO) that provides guidance, templates, and best practices but does not directly control project execution. What type of PMO is this? *

o.t: Supportive PMO
Controlling PMO
Directive PMO
Hybrid PMO

questions.e: A Supportive PMO primarily acts as a consultative body, offering guidance, templates, training, and best practices while allowing project managers full autonomy over their projects. This type of PMO is best suited for organizations with a decentralized project management structure where teams require minimal oversight.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered an Organizational Process Asset (OPA) rather than an Enterprise Environmental Factor (EEF)? *

o.t: Industry standards and regulatory requirements.
Project closure documents and lessons learned from past projects.
Political climate affecting project execution.
Market trends influencing project budgets.

questions.e: Organizational Process Assets (OPAs) are internal assets that help improve project execution and are controlled by the organization. These include: Historical project data (e.g., lessons learned, past project reports). Templates and standard procedures (e.g., risk registers, checklists). Knowledge bases and best practices. The other options are Enterprise Environmental Factors (EEFs), as they are external influences that cannot be controlled by the project team.

questions.q: A project’s business case includes a sensitivity analysis to account for uncertainty in financial projections. Which of the following best describes the purpose of sensitivity analysis in a business case? *

o.t: To evaluate how changes in key assumptions (e.g., costs, revenue, risks) impact project feasibility.
To determine the minimum funding required for the project.
To compare financial metrics such as IRR and NPV under fixed assumptions.
To assess the expected duration of project benefits before obsolescence.

questions.e: Sensitivity analysis tests how different assumptions impact project outcomes. It helps decision-makers understand which variables have the greatest effect on project success. This is crucial in business case development, as market conditions, costs, and revenues are often uncertain. Financial projections are only as reliable as their assumptions, so sensitivity analysis provides a range of possible outcomes to support informed decision-making. By running "what-if" scenarios, organizations can better prepare for risks and uncertainties in project execution.

questions.q: Which stakeholder analysis technique is best for mapping stakeholders based on their power, urgency, and legitimacy in relation to the project? *

o.t: Power/Interest Grid
Stakeholder Cube
Salience Model
Influence/Impact Matrix

questions.e: The Salience Model assesses stakeholders based on three attributes: power, urgency, and legitimacy. This model helps project managers prioritize stakeholders effectively.

questions.q: Which stakeholder identification tool helps determine the responsibilities, authority, and influence of stakeholders in a structured format? *

o.t: Power/Interest Grid
RACI Matrix
Stakeholder Register
Communication Plan

questions.e: The RACI Matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) clarifies stakeholder roles and responsibilities in project activities, helping to ensure effective engagement and accountability.

questions.q: A project manager wants to evaluate how different stakeholder engagement strategies are performing. Which tool is most useful? *

o.t: Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix
Issue Log
Change Control Board
RACI Matrix

questions.e: The Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix compares current vs. desired engagement levels and helps assess whether engagement strategies need adjustment.

questions.q: A project has multiple stakeholders with conflicting interests. The project sponsor prioritizes cost savings, while the end users are concerned about usability and features. How should you handle this situation? *

o.t: Focus on satisfying the project sponsor since they have more authority.
Conduct stakeholder workshops to find a balanced solution.
Ignore the end users' concerns since they are not funding the project.
Delay the project until all stakeholders agree on a common goal.

questions.e: Stakeholder conflicts should be resolved through collaboration and negotiation. Workshops help align expectations and develop a mutually beneficial approach without compromising project success.

questions.q: A project team member informs you that an important stakeholder is spreading misinformation about the project, which could damage credibility. What should you do? *

o.t: Confront the stakeholder publicly to correct the misinformation.
Meet privately with the stakeholder to clarify misunderstandings.
Issue a formal email to all stakeholders correcting the misinformation.
Ignore the situation, assuming the truth will emerge over time.

questions.e: Stakeholders may unintentionally spread incorrect information. A private meeting allows you to clarify and correct misunderstandings without escalating the conflict.

questions.q: A project team is experiencing frequent conflicts due to different working styles. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Ignore the conflicts unless they impact project performance.
Conduct a team-building exercise to improve communication and understanding.
Assign tasks based on working style preferences to avoid clashes.
Replace team members who are causing disruptions.

questions.e: Conflicts arising from different working styles can be mitigated through team-building activities that foster trust, communication, and adaptability.

questions.q: A project manager has authority over salary increases, promotions, and recognition programs. They use this to motivate the team by offering incentives for high performance. What type of power is this? *

o.t: Reward Power
Legitimate Power
Coercive Power
Referent Power

questions.e: Reward power is based on the ability to give incentives such as bonuses, promotions, or public recognition. This power is often used to motivate and reinforce positive behavior.

questions.q: According to Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following would be classified as a hygiene factor rather than a motivator? *

o.t: Recognition for achievements
Opportunities for personal growth
Job security and salary
Challenging work assignments

questions.e: Hygiene factors (e.g., salary, job security, company policies) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate employees. Motivators (e.g., recognition, growth, challenging work) increase job satisfaction and drive motivation.

questions.q: A project manager notices that some employees feel demotivated because they perceive that their peers are receiving better rewards for similar work. Which motivation theory explains this? *

o.t: Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory
Equity Theory
McGregor’s Theory X
Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs

questions.e: Equity Theory states that employees compare their effort and rewards to those of others. If they perceive unfairness, motivation decreases, leading to dissatisfaction.

questions.q: A junior project team member complains that a senior team member is dismissing their ideas during discussions. The junior member is becoming disengaged, and their performance is declining. What is the best way to handle this situation? *

o.t: Arrange a private discussion with the senior member to correct their behavior.
Hold a team-building session focused on respectful collaboration.
Meet with both team members together to facilitate an open discussion.
Tell the junior team member to adapt and be more assertive.

questions.e: A facilitated discussion allows both team members to express their concerns and find a constructive way to collaborate. Only addressing the senior member (A) does not promote teamwork. A general team-building session (B) may help in the long run but does not directly resolve the conflict. Telling the junior member to be more assertive (D) ignores the underlying issue of respect and collaboration.

questions.q: During an Agile sprint, a team member identifies a potential risk that could impact the project timeline. What should the team do next? *

o.t: Immediately escalate the risk to the product owner and wait for a decision.
Address the risk in the daily stand-up and discuss mitigation strategies as a team.
Pause the sprint and conduct a full risk assessment before continuing.
Document the risk but wait until the sprint retrospective to discuss it.

questions.e: Agile teams are self-organizing and proactive in risk management. The daily stand-up is an opportunity to discuss roadblocks and risks, allowing the team to collaboratively find solutions. Escalation (A) without team discussion contradicts Agile's empowered team approach. Pausing the sprint (C) is unnecessary. Waiting until the retrospective (D) could delay mitigation.

questions.q: A project team using an Agile framework delivers new product features every two weeks. The team follows a consistent schedule and does not release changes outside of this fixed interval. What type of delivery cadence is this? *

o.t: Iteration-Based Delivery
Continuous Deployment
Flow-Based Delivery
Rolling-Wave Planning

questions.e: Iteration-Based Delivery follows a fixed cadence (e.g., every two weeks, every month) and aligns with frameworks like Scrum. Continuous Deployment (B) releases updates immediately after validation, rather than waiting for a fixed time window. Flow-Based Delivery (C) is used in Kanban, where work is released as soon as it is ready, rather than in scheduled iterations. Rolling-Wave Planning (D) is a progressive elaboration technique, not a delivery cadence.

questions.q: The Development Team has identified a critical technical debt issue during a Sprint. How should this be handled? *

o.t: Log it in the Product Backlog and address it in a future Sprint.
Immediately stop work on Sprint items and resolve the technical debt.
Extend the Sprint length to accommodate technical debt resolution.
Escalate to the Product Owner for immediate prioritization.

questions.e: Technical debt should be tracked and addressed in future Sprints based on priority. Interrupting the Sprint disrupts focus and delivery.

questions.q: During Sprint Planning, the Scrum Team is struggling to determine how much work they can commit to. What technique can help them make a more informed decision? *

o.t: Use velocity from previous Sprints as a guideline for commitment.
Assign backlog items based on individual availability rather than team velocity.
Set a fixed number of story points per Sprint regardless of past performance.
Ask the Scrum Master to determine the commitment level for the team.

questions.e: Past velocity helps teams set realistic expectations and commitments, ensuring sustainable development.

questions.q: A company has successfully tested an MVP with a small group of early adopters. Now, they want to release a version with enough functionality to attract a broader customer base and generate revenue. What should they focus on developing next? *

o.t: Expand the MVP with minor improvements and keep testing.
Develop the Minimum Marketable Product (MMP) with core features that deliver customer value.
Scale up immediately and build a fully featured product.
Conduct additional market research before making any changes.

questions.e: The MMP is the version of the product that is ready for commercial release with features that attract paying customers. Expanding the MVP (A) indefinitely delays market entry. Scaling up too soon (C) increases risk without validation. Market research (D) is important but should not delay a validated product launch.

questions.q: During project execution, the project team discovers that several activities are taking longer than originally estimated, causing a schedule delay. The project sponsor insists that the project must still finish on the original deadline. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Perform a schedule variance analysis against the Schedule Baseline and identify possible corrective actions.
Immediately crash the schedule by adding more resources to recover lost time.
Request an immediate baseline update to reflect the new timeline.
Ignore the delay, as the team might naturally catch up later in execution.

questions.e: Before taking action, the project manager must analyze the Schedule Baseline to understand the root cause of the delays. Possible corrective actions include: Fast tracking (rearranging tasks to run in parallel where feasible). Crashing (adding resources, but only if it doesn’t cause inefficiencies). Reassessing dependencies and constraints to optimize workflow. Updating the baseline (C) is inappropriate without a formal change request and impact assessment. Ignoring the delay (D) is risky and may result in a missed deadline.

questions.q: What is the primary disadvantage of using the Waterfall methodology in software development projects? *

o.t: It requires constant customer involvement throughout the project.
Changes to requirements are difficult to implement after the design phase.
It lacks a clear structure for tracking project progress.
It allows for too much flexibility, making it hard to define project scope.

questions.e: Since Waterfall follows a sequential approach, changes to requirements late in the process are costly and disruptive. Option A is an Agile characteristic. Option C is incorrect; Waterfall has structured tracking. Option D is false, as Waterfall is rigid.

questions.q: A Waterfall project has a detailed project schedule, but a key supplier notifies the team of a late delivery, which will impact critical path activities. What is the best way to handle this situation? *

o.t: Use schedule compression techniques like crashing or fast-tracking.
Extend the project deadline to accommodate the delay.
Replace the supplier immediately with a new vendor.
Ignore the delay, assuming other activities will make up for lost time.

questions.e: Crashing (adding resources) or Fast-Tracking (overlapping activities) are schedule compression techniques used to mitigate delays affecting the critical path. Option B delays project completion. Option C may cause additional risks and costs. Option D assumes without validating, which is poor risk management.

questions.q: A project is being executed using a Hybrid methodology, where Agile teams handle development while a Waterfall framework manages regulatory compliance. A key stakeholder insists on having a detailed, fixed-scope project plan with milestone dates, but the Agile teams operate using iterative releases. How should the project manager address this conflict? *

o.t: Create a dual reporting structure where Agile teams use burndown charts, and the Waterfall plan includes milestone tracking for stakeholders.
Force the Agile teams to adopt a fully predictive model to meet stakeholder expectations.
Ask the stakeholder to accept a purely Agile approach and remove fixed milestone expectations.
Require the Agile teams to complete all development work upfront before regulatory reviews begin.

questions.e: In Hybrid project management, different reporting methods help balance Agile iteration flexibility with Waterfall's structured milestone tracking. Forcing Agile into Waterfall (B) removes the benefits of iteration and responsiveness. Removing milestones (C) is unrealistic for regulatory compliance. Developing everything before regulatory review (D) causes delays and prevents iterative feedback.

questions.q: A project is in the execution phase when a key stakeholder requests a significant change to the project scope. The change would impact the timeline and budget. What is the first step the project manager should take? *

o.t: Implement the change immediately to meet stakeholder expectations.
Refer the request to the Change Control Board (CCB) for approval.
Conduct an impact analysis to evaluate the effect on scope, schedule, and cost.
Reject the change request because it was not part of the original plan.

questions.e: Before escalating a change request to the Change Control Board (CCB), the project manager must assess its impact. Impact analysis helps determine feasibility, risks, and necessary adjustments. Implementing changes without evaluation (A) leads to uncontrolled scope creep. Escalating to the CCB (B) is premature without impact assessment. Rejecting changes outright (D) may not align with business needs.

questions.q: A project manager needs to collect requirements from a dispersed group of experts while avoiding the influence of dominant participants. Which technique is most suitable? *

o.t: Delphi Technique
Focus Groups
Requirements Workshops
Benchmarking

questions.e: Delphi Technique gathers expert opinions anonymously, reducing bias and ensuring balanced input from all participants. Focus Groups (B) involve interactive discussions but are subject to dominant personalities. Requirements Workshops (C) allow collaboration but do not eliminate bias. Benchmarking (D) compares against industry best practices but does not collect original requirements.

questions.q: Which requirement collection technique uses visual representations to clarify relationships between different system components? *

o.t: Context Diagrams
Document Analysis
Delphi Technique
Brainstorming

questions.e: Context diagrams visually depict system interactions, helping stakeholders understand data flows and dependencies. Document Analysis (B) reviews records but does not create visual representations. Delphi Technique (C) collects expert feedback but does not create diagrams. Brainstorming (D) generates ideas but does not map system relationships.

questions.q: A project team is estimating the effort required for a software project based on the number of lines of code. Which estimating technique is being used? *

o.t: Analogous Estimating
Bottom-Up Estimating
Parametric Estimating
Expert Judgment

questions.e: Parametric estimating uses statistical relationships between variables, such as cost per unit or effort per deliverable, making it ideal for productivity-based estimates. Analogous estimating (A) uses historical project comparisons rather than unit metrics. Bottom-up estimating (B) aggregates individual estimates but does not rely on mathematical relationships. Expert judgment (D) relies on experience rather than statistical modeling.

questions.q: A team estimates that a construction project will cost $100 per square foot based on industry benchmarks. Which technique is being used? *

o.t: Parametric Estimating
Bottom-Up Estimating
Heuristic Estimating
Analogous Estimating

questions.e: Parametric estimating applies statistical relationships (e.g., cost per unit) to estimate total project costs. Bottom-up estimating (B) calculates task-level costs rather than using unit rates. Heuristic estimating (C) uses general rules but is not unit-based. Analogous estimating (D) compares past projects rather than applying cost-per-unit data.

questions.q: A project sponsor wants to ensure full alignment before finalizing a key decision. The project team discusses all options thoroughly until every member agrees on the final choice. What type of voting technique is this? *

o.t: Unanimity
Plurality Voting
Majority Voting
Delphi Technique

questions.e: Unanimity means all participants must agree on the decision before proceeding. Plurality (B) selects the option with the most votes, even if not all agree. Majority voting (C) only requires more than 50% agreement. Delphi Technique (D) is an anonymous expert consensus method, not open discussion.

questions.q: A development team collaboratively works on the same task at the same time using one workstation. What technique are they using? *

o.t: Mobbing
Swarming
Pair Programming
Fast Tracking

questions.e: Mobbing involves the whole team working together on a single task at one workstation. Swarming (B) refers to multiple people addressing the same issue but working separately. Pair programming (C) involves two developers, not an entire team. Fast tracking (D) speeds up project tasks but does not involve collaborative execution.

questions.q: A project team delays starting critical tasks until the last possible moment, creating unnecessary schedule risks. What is this an example of? *

o.t: Student Syndrome
Parkinson’s Law
Fast Tracking
Sandbagging

questions.e: Student Syndrome describes the tendency to procrastinate until a deadline is near, creating last-minute pressure. Parkinson’s Law (B) relates to work expanding to fit time, not procrastination. Fast Tracking (C) is a schedule compression technique. Sandbagging (D) involves under-promising to exceed expectations.

questions.q: A team is assigned multiple tasks, but instead of focusing on completing one before starting another, they keep switching between tasks. This leads to delays and inefficiencies. What is this an example of? *

o.t: Multitasking
Swarming
Mobbing
Fast Tracking

questions.e: Multitasking leads to inefficiency because of frequent context switching, reducing focus and productivity. Swarming (B) involves multiple people working on the same issue together. Mobbing (C) is extreme collaboration on a single task. Fast Tracking (D) overlaps tasks to accelerate project delivery.

questions.q: After a major project failure, an organization conducts a detailed lessons learned review. However, when a similar project is initiated a year later, the same mistakes are repeated. What should be done differently? *

o.t: Incorporate the lessons learned into training programs and standard operating procedures (SOPs).
Conduct a more detailed failure analysis to identify deeper root causes.
Assign the same project manager to ensure previous mistakes are avoided.
Make project managers accountable for reviewing past project failures before starting new ones.

questions.e: Lessons learned must be institutionalized through training and SOPs to prevent repeated mistakes. Conducting more analysis (B) is useful but does not ensure corrective action. Assigning the same project manager (C) does not guarantee systemic improvements. Making PMs accountable (D) helps but does not embed changes into processes.

questions.q: A project team is experiencing frequent delays due to waiting for approvals. What should the project manager do to improve execution efficiency? *

o.t: Increase the frequency of meetings with stakeholders to get approvals faster.
Delegate approval authority to team leads when possible.
Implement a stricter deadline for approvals.
Escalate the issue to the project sponsor.

questions.e: Empowering team leads speeds up decision-making without bottlenecks. More meetings (A) increase administrative burden. Stricter deadlines (C) may cause rushed or uninformed decisions. Escalation (D) should be a last resort.

questions.q: During a bidder conference, a vendor tries to persuade the project manager by offering additional services at a discounted rate. How should the project manager respond? *

o.t: Accept the offer if it benefits the project.
Inform all bidders about the offer to maintain fairness.
Reject the offer and remind the vendor that the bidding process must remain fair.
Allow the vendor to submit an updated proposal after the conference.

questions.e: Bidder conferences must remain neutral. Offering additional services during the meeting could lead to an unfair selection process. Informing all bidders (B) does not address the fairness concern directly. Accepting the offer (A, D) violates procurement integrity.

questions.q: A project manager is reviewing vendor proposals and realizes that vendors have submitted different formats, making it difficult to compare them. What should the project manager have done to ensure a fair vendor evaluation? *

o.t: Require vendors to submit proposals in a standard template.
Allow flexibility in proposal formats to encourage creativity.
Select the vendor with the most detailed proposal.
Request additional information from selected vendors only.

questions.e: A standard template ensures consistency, making it easier to compare vendor proposals. Allowing flexibility (B) can lead to inconsistent data. Selecting based on proposal detail (C) ignores fair evaluation principles. Requesting additional info only from some vendors (D) creates bias.

questions.q: A vendor agrees to deliver a software product for a fixed price but will receive an additional payment if delivery is completed early. What contract type is being used? *

o.t: Cost Plus Award Fee (CPAF)
Firm Fixed Price (FFP)
Fixed Price Incentive Fee (FPIF)
Cost Plus Fixed Fee (CPFF)

questions.e: FPIF contracts offer a fixed price plus performance-based incentives, such as early delivery bonuses. CPAF (A) offers bonuses but is cost-reimbursable, not fixed price. FFP (B) has no incentives—just a set price. CPFF (D) reimburses costs plus a fixed fee, not performance-based bonuses.

questions.q: A project vendor is consistently missing delivery deadlines, impacting the project schedule. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Issue a formal warning and apply penalties as per the contract.
Meet with the vendor to understand the cause of delays and find a resolution.
Terminate the contract and find a new vendor.
Request senior management to intervene in vendor operations.

questions.e: Engaging the vendor to identify issues helps address delays collaboratively before taking strict actions. Issuing penalties (A) should come after discussions fail. Terminating the contract (C) is a last resort. Senior management intervention (D) is unnecessary at this stage.

questions.q: A project manager is working with multiple vendors and wants to ensure contract compliance throughout execution. What is the best approach? *

o.t: Conduct regular contract performance reviews.
Require vendors to submit weekly progress reports.
Escalate any vendor issues to procurement management.
Apply penalties for any minor contract deviations.

questions.e: Regular reviews ensure compliance and prevent issues from escalating. Weekly reports (B) provide updates but do not replace full compliance checks. Escalation (C) should be reserved for major issues. Strict penalties (D) may harm vendor relationships.

questions.q: A project team documents best practices and lessons learned from quality control inspections to improve future processes. What quality technique is being used? *

o.t: Continuous Improvement (Kaizen)
Statistical Process Control
Pareto Analysis
Control Charts

questions.e: Kaizen promotes incremental process improvements using feedback and best practices. Statistical Process Control (B) monitors process variations. Pareto Analysis (C) prioritizes issues but does not emphasize ongoing improvement. Control Charts (D) track stability but do not promote process enhancement.

questions.q: A project team wants to analyze the distribution of defects by category to determine which type occurs most frequently. What tool should they use? *

o.t: Histogram
Scatter Diagram
Fishbone Diagram
Control Chart

questions.e: Histograms show the frequency of defects by category, helping teams prioritize corrections. Scatter Diagrams (B) analyze correlations, not distributions. Fishbone Diagrams (C) identify root causes. Control Charts (D) track variations over time.

questions.q: A project manager wants to ensure that vendors comply with the company’s quality management standards. What is the best approach? *

o.t: Conduct regular supplier quality audits
Increase the frequency of product testing
Require vendors to submit more detailed reports
Replace vendors who have past quality issues

questions.e: Supplier quality audits help verify that vendors follow quality standards and processes. Increasing testing (B) detects issues but does not ensure compliance. Requiring more reports (C) does not guarantee quality improvement. Replacing vendors (D) should be a last resort after corrective actions fail.

questions.q: A project team is conducting frequent quality inspections and product testing. While this ensures defects are detected early, the project manager is concerned about rising costs. What type of cost is increasing? *

o.t: Prevention Costs
Appraisal Costs
Internal Failure Costs
External Failure Costs

questions.e: Appraisal costs cover inspections, testing, and quality audits. Prevention costs (A) involve training and process improvements. Internal failure costs (C) occur when defects are detected before product delivery. External failure costs (D) arise from defects after delivery.

questions.q: A project sponsor requests faster delivery of a product without increasing costs. The project manager is concerned that this will affect quality. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Agree to the request but increase inspections to catch defects.
Conduct a cost-benefit analysis to evaluate the impact of speeding up delivery.
Increase team workload to meet the deadline without affecting quality.
Reduce quality standards to accommodate the faster delivery.

questions.e: A cost-benefit analysis helps assess trade-offs between speed, cost, and quality before making a decision. Increasing inspections (A) adds costs but does not prevent defects. Increasing workload (C) may lead to burnout and quality issues. Reducing quality standards (D) compromises project deliverables.

questions.q: A project manager is developing the risk management plan and needs to define how often risk assessments will take place. What factor should most influence this decision? *

o.t: The project budget and cost constraints.
The project’s complexity, industry, and level of uncertainty.
The availability of project team members.
The number of risks identified during planning.

questions.e: Frequent risk assessments are essential for complex, high-uncertainty projects. Budget constraints (A) should not prevent necessary risk reviews. Availability of team members (C) should not dictate how risks are managed. The number of risks (D) is important but does not replace industry best practices.

questions.q: A project manager is aware that there may be delays due to uncertain weather conditions during an outdoor construction project. The project team cannot predict exactly when or how severe these delays will be, but they know the risk exists. What type of risk does this represent? *

o.t: Known Unknown
Unknown Unknown
Residual Risk
Secondary Risk

questions.e: Known unknowns are risks that have been identified, but their exact impact and timing remain uncertain. In this case, the project team knows bad weather could cause delays, but they cannot predict exactly when or how severe it will be. Unknown unknowns (B) are completely unforeseen risks. Residual risks (C) remain after risk responses have been implemented. Secondary risks (D) arise as a result of implementing a risk response.

questions.q: A multinational project team is working on an artificial intelligence (AI) development initiative. The project involves integrating data from multiple countries, each with its own regulations and privacy laws. The team is struggling to manage different compliance requirements and technological dependencies. Which element is creating the biggest challenge? *

o.t: Volatility
Uncertainty
Complexity
Ambiguity

questions.e: Complexity arises when a project involves multiple interdependent factors, such as regulatory variations, diverse stakeholders, and cross-border technology integration. Volatility (A) would apply if the external environment was changing unpredictably, but the main challenge here is managing multiple interdependencies. Uncertainty (B) involves a lack of clarity about future outcomes, whereas in this case, the issue is understanding and managing multiple regulations. Ambiguity (D) relates to unclear or undefined scenarios, whereas the issue here is too many interconnected elements.

questions.q: During project execution, a new government regulation is introduced that affects project compliance requirements. The project team had not identified this risk during planning. What should the project manager do first? *

o.t: Escalate the issue to senior management for a decision.
Conduct a risk reassessment and update the risk register.
Proceed with the original plan and address compliance later.
Terminate the project as compliance changes were not accounted for.

questions.e: Risk reassessment is essential when new risks emerge. Escalating immediately (A) may be premature without analyzing the impact. Ignoring compliance (C) could lead to legal consequences. Project termination (D) should be a last resort after thorough analysis.

questions.q: A project risk register contains multiple risks, but the project sponsor is only concerned about risks that could delay the project's completion date. What tool should the project manager use to prioritize risks based on schedule impact? *

o.t: Monte Carlo Simulation
Sensitivity Analysis (Tornado Diagram)
Risk Probability and Impact Matrix
Earned Value Management (EVM)

questions.e: Sensitivity analysis identifies which risks have the greatest impact on project objectives (e.g., schedule). Monte Carlo Simulation (A) models overall project uncertainty but does not focus only on schedule risks. Probability and Impact Matrix (C) helps prioritize risks but does not analyze schedule impact specifically. EVM (D) measures cost and schedule performance but does not analyze risks.

questions.q: A company is evaluating multiple project proposals and wants to select the one with the highest potential return on investment. Which financial metric should they prioritize if they want to measure the profitability of each project over time? *

o.t: Net Present Value (NPV)
Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
Payback Period
Cost Variance (CV)

questions.e: IRR is the discount rate at which the net present value (NPV) of a project becomes zero, effectively measuring the project's profitability over time. NPV (A) calculates the total value of future cash flows in today’s terms but does not express profitability as a percentage. Payback Period (C) measures how long it takes to recover the initial investment but does not indicate profitability. CV (D) is a cost performance metric, not an investment analysis tool.

questions.q: A project manager prepares a weekly status report for stakeholders. One of the stakeholders complains that the report contains too much technical detail and is difficult to understand. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Stop sending the report to that stakeholder.
Adjust the report format to include both summary and detailed sections.
Reduce the report to one page without technical information.
Tell the stakeholder to ignore the technical details.

questions.e: A well-structured report should include a high-level summary for non-technical stakeholders while keeping detailed sections for technical readers. Stopping the report (A) ignores stakeholder needs. Reducing it to one page (C) may remove important information. Telling the stakeholder to ignore details (D) is unprofessional and ineffective.

questions.q: A company wants to measure how effectively its employees are contributing to project success. Which metric should they use? *

o.t: Resource Utilization Rate
Velocity
Team Happiness
Turnover Rate

questions.e: Resource Utilization Rate measures how efficiently human resources are being used in a project.

questions.q: A project manager is trying to determine the estimated funds required to complete the remaining work on a project. Which formula should they use? *

o.t: EAC = BAC / CPI
EV = PV × % Complete
ETC = EAC - AC
SPI = EV / PV

questions.e: ETC (Estimate to Complete) tells how much more is needed to finish the project. ETC = EAC - AC, where: EAC is the estimated total cost of the project. AC is the cost incurred so far.

questions.q: A project is ahead of schedule but over budget. What would be the most likely values for SPI and CPI? *

o.t: SPI > 1, CPI > 1
SPI < 1, CPI < 1
SPI > 1, CPI < 1
SPI < 1, CPI > 1

questions.e: SPI > 1 means the project is ahead of schedule. CPI < 1 means the project is over budget.

questions.q: During project execution, a senior stakeholder requests a major change that could impact project scope. What is your next step? *

o.t: Implement the change to maintain stakeholder satisfaction.
Direct the team to stop work until the change is analyzed.
Submit the change request for impact assessment.
Inform the stakeholder that changes are not allowed in execution.

questions.e: All scope changes must go through the integrated change control process. Option A (implementing immediately) risks scope creep. Option B (stopping work) is not necessary unless the change is critical. Option D (rejecting the change outright) ignores stakeholder needs.

questions.q: A project has multiple external vendors. One vendor consistently fails to meet deadlines, causing delays. What should you do first? *

o.t: Terminate the contract and find a new vendor.
Meet with the vendor to discuss performance issues and corrective actions.
Escalate the issue to senior management.
Reduce the scope of work assigned to the vendor.

questions.e: Vendor performance issues should first be addressed through direct communication before contract termination. Escalation (C) and scope reduction (D) may be considered if the vendor fails to improve.

questions.q: A project team is struggling with communication breakdowns due to team members being in different time zones. What should the project manager do? *

o.t: Schedule all meetings at a fixed time convenient for the project manager.
Use asynchronous communication tools and flexible meeting schedules.
Require all team members to adjust to a single time zone.
Assign separate project managers for different time zones.

questions.e: Distributed teams benefit from communication tools like Slack, Trello, and recorded meetings. Forcing a single time zone (C) reduces productivity. Separate project managers (D) is unnecessary for one project.

questions.q: The project is completed, and the client is satisfied. What should the project manager do next? *

o.t: Release the team and move to a new project.
Conduct a lessons learned session and update project records.
Send a final invoice and close the project immediately.
Archive only financial records for future reference.

questions.e: A project is not fully closed until lessons learned are captured and documentation is completed. Releasing the team (A) should happen after formal closure. Sending invoices (C) is necessary, but project closure is broader. Archiving only financial records (D) ignores other important documentation.

questions.q: A stakeholder prefers detailed reports on progress, but the development team follows an Agile methodology with minimal documentation. What is the best hybrid approach? *

o.t: Provide high-level progress reports while keeping Agile documentation minimal.
Force the team to follow Waterfall documentation standards.
Ask the stakeholder to adapt to Agile ways of working.
Ignore documentation requirements to maintain Agile speed.

questions.e: A hybrid approach balances stakeholder needs with Agile flexibility. Option B (full Waterfall documentation) may burden the Agile team. Option C (forcing stakeholder adaptation) may reduce engagement. Option D (ignoring documentation needs) risks stakeholder dissatisfaction.
